raw_question: How much of the observed respiratory activity and feeding reduction can be attributed to the warm-up, falling DO, or TAN change, and which readings are only associated observations?
evidence_gaps: Scheduled readings leave the timing and daily minimum of temperature and DO uncertain. No pH or unionized-ammonia result is available to interpret the TAN increase. There are no continuous measurements, comparison raceway, or untreated interval, and aeration, ration reduction, and water exchange occurred close together. The continued incomplete feeding on 5 August also means the duration of recovery is not established.
fish_response: Faster gill movement and reduced feed response were first noted during the morning check on 4 August, after the recorded temperature rise and DO decline. No mortality was recorded. By 5 August, surface activity was reduced, but the ration was still not fully consumed.
possible_causes: The rapid temperature increase is a plausible contributor because it preceded the fish observations and coincided with declining DO. Lower DO could have contributed to increased respiratory effort, while warmer water may increase oxygen demand and reduce oxygen availability. The TAN increase is also a candidate change, but its toxic significance cannot be determined from this record because pH and unionized ammonia were not measured. Stable flow and nearly unchanged nitrite-N provide little support for those factors as primary causes.
raw_case_record: Raceway B-2 log, 3–5 August. At 06:00 on 3 August, water temperature was 13.2°C, DO 8.0 mg/L, TAN 0.16 mg/L, nitrite-N 0.03 mg/L, and flow 100% of the usual rate. At 18:00, temperature was 15.1°C and DO 7.2 mg/L; flow remained 99%. At 06:00 on 4 August, temperature was 17.8°C, DO 6.1 mg/L, TAN 0.39 mg/L, nitrite-N 0.04 mg/L, and flow 100%. Staff noted faster gill movement and reduced feed response beginning during the morning check; the previous day's ration had been consumed normally. No mortality was recorded. At 10:00, staff added backup aeration. At 12:00, the ration was reduced by one-third. At 14:00, a 10% water exchange was made using the available supply water, measured at 16.8°C. At 06:00 on 5 August, tank temperature was 16.9°C, DO 7.0 mg/L, TAN 0.31 mg/L, nitrite-N 0.04 mg/L, and flow 99%. Fish were less reactive at the surface, but the morning ration was still not fully consumed. Tank pH and unionized ammonia were not measured. Temperature and chemistry readings were taken at scheduled checks rather than continuously.
causal_mechanism: A warmer tank can increase fish metabolic oxygen demand while reducing oxygen availability in water; the concurrent DO decline could therefore have contributed to faster gill movement. Stress associated with these conditions could also reduce feeding. TAN rose, but without pH and unionized-ammonia measurements its contribution cannot be assessed from the record. The subsequent partial improvement followed several simultaneous management actions, so it is consistent with mitigation but does not confirm a single causal pathway.
timeline_summary: On 3 August, temperature rose from 13.2°C at 06:00 to 15.1°C by 18:00 while DO fell from 8.0 to 7.2 mg/L; flow remained near its usual rate. By 06:00 on 4 August, temperature was 17.8°C, DO 6.1 mg/L, and TAN 0.39 mg/L. Faster gill movement and reduced feed response were noted that morning. Backup aeration, a reduced ration, and a 10% water exchange followed. On 5 August, temperature and TAN were lower and DO higher; surface activity was reduced, but feeding had not fully returned to normal. No mortality was recorded.
diagnostic_answer: The warm-up and concurrent DO decline are the most plausible contributors to the faster gill movement, with reduced feeding a likely accompanying stress response. The rise in TAN is a possible additional factor, but it cannot be linked confidently without pH or unionized-ammonia data. Flow was stable and nitrite-N changed little, so neither is strongly implicated by these observations. The improvement after aeration and water exchange is compatible with reduced stress, but multiple actions were taken together and measurements were intermittent; causation remains plausible rather than confirmed.
management_actions: Backup aeration was added at 10:00 on 4 August. At 12:00, staff reduced the ration by one-third. A 10% water exchange using 16.8°C supply water was completed at 14:00. The following morning's readings showed higher DO and lower temperature and TAN, but feeding remained below normal.
water_quality_changes: Over roughly 24 hours, temperature increased from 13.2°C to 17.8°C, while DO declined from 8.0 to 6.1 mg/L. TAN rose from 0.16 to 0.39 mg/L by the morning of 4 August and was 0.31 mg/L on 5 August. Nitrite-N changed only from 0.03 to 0.04 mg/L. Flow stayed at 99–100% of its usual rate. After aeration and a 10% exchange with 16.8°C supply water, the 5 August readings were 16.9°C and 7.0 mg/L DO. Measurements were scheduled rather than continuous; pH and unionized ammonia were not measured.
accompanying_phenomena: The TAN rise occurred during the same period as the temperature and DO changes, but the record does not establish that it caused the response. Reduced feeding was observed alongside respiratory activity and may be a consequence of stress; the later ration reduction was a management response, not evidence of the initiating cause. Improvement after 5 August followed aeration, reduced feeding, and water exchange together, so it cannot be assigned to any one action.
